The central question is whether sliding-window attention mechanisms, when used as context compression under long-document retrieval, systematically destroy the semantic structures that retrieval was meant to preserve — not randomly, but at predictable eviction boundaries where coherent spans get split mid-argument, mid-entity-chain, or mid-coreference arc. The key concepts are: attention sinks (the pathological concentration of attention weight on early tokens — typically BOS or positional anchors — that causes those tokens to be retained under eviction scoring heuristics regardless of semantic content); token eviction bias (the tendency of importance-score-based eviction policies to preferentially drop tokens that lack high local attention weight but carry critical bridging semantics — connectives, anaphora, discourse markers); and semantic coherence collapse (the phase-transition-like degradation that occurs not gradually but abruptly when a compressed context loses the span that resolves a referent or anchors a logical chain). The beginner assumes eviction error is proportional to eviction volume — drop 20% of tokens, lose roughly 20% of information — but the expert knows the relationship is sharply nonlinear: coherence can survive aggressive compression until a single critical token is evicted, at which point downstream retrieval quality collapses discontinuously. What practitioners consistently underestimate is that attention sink tokens actively crowd out semantically load-bearing tokens during retention scoring, meaning the eviction policy's internal ranking is structurally corrupted — not just noisy — by the sink's artificial importance inflation, and this corruption worsens as document length increases because sinks accumulate proportionally more attention mass in longer contexts.

A token is coherence-critical when it serves as a resolution anchor for downstream spans — concretely, when removing it forces a language model to hallucinate or abstain on a coreference, bridging inference, or entity-tracking query that depends on it. The three operationalizable properties are: (1) high out-degree in the attention graph across multiple layers (the token is attended to by many future tokens, not just attending outward), (2) low local attention weight received in the current window (making it invisible to standard importance scorers like H2O's heavy-hitter oracle, which ranks by cumulative attention mass received), and (3) positional isolation — the token sits at a discourse boundary where no paraphrase or redundant restatement exists within the retained window. To probe for these offline, you'd run a causal token ablation sweep: for each candidate eviction token, mask it, re-run the forward pass on a fixed downstream query set, and measure KL divergence between the masked and unmasked output distributions — tokens producing KL > some threshold ε are flagged as coherence-critical; Shi et al.'s "Retrieval Head" work (2024) essentially applies this logic at the head level and finds that fewer than 5% of attention heads account for the majority of retrieval-sensitive information propagation. A cheaper proxy is gradient-weighted attention (GradCAM-style): backpropagate from a retrieval-sensitive loss signal through the attention weights to get a saliency score per token that correlates with eviction risk better than forward-pass attention mass alone — though this still requires a labeled query to define the loss. The deep pathology is that H2O, SnapKV, and similar systems rank tokens by how much attention they attract, which anti-correlates with coherence-criticality for bridging tokens: a discourse connective like "however" or a null-subject pronoun receives almost no attention in a window where its referent has already been established locally, yet its absence in a compressed context causes catastrophic referent drift when that window is later retrieved.

Positional entropy of incoming attention across layers also serves as a query-agnostic proxy — tokens that receive attention from maximally dispersed future positions carry information needed by many downstream spans, and this signal is computable purely from the forward pass without any query. The fundamental limitation experts navigate is that query-agnostic criticality scoring has irreducible false negatives: some tokens are critical only conditionally on a narrow query class, and no structural probe catches them without implicit query distribution assumptions — which is why systems like MagicPID (2024) hedge by retaining tokens above a structural threshold plus a small query-specific cache populated lazily at retrieval time.

When a coreference chain is split at an eviction boundary, the retained half presents the model with an unresolved referent — a pronoun, definite NP, or zero-anaphor whose antecedent no longer exists in the active context window, forcing the model into one of three pathological behaviors: (1) spurious resolution, where the model binds the dangling referent to the nearest semantically plausible entity in the retained window (which may be a different entity entirely), (2) referent invention, where the model hallucinates an antecedent consistent with the retained context, or (3) referent collapse, where repeated references to the evicted entity get silently merged with another entity's representation, corrupting all downstream attribute-tracking for both entities. The insidious property of spurious resolution is that it produces fluent, confident, wrong output — the model doesn't signal uncertainty because its local context is internally consistent after the false binding; this is why perplexity on the retained window is a useless failure detector here. Pre-generation detection is possible via entity continuity probing: before generation, run a lightweight forward pass that checks whether every definite NP and pronoun in the retained context can be resolved to an antecedent within that context using a coref head or a probing classifier trained on entity-tracking tasks — Wu et al.'s entity tracking work (2022) shows that transformer hidden states encode entity identity reliably enough that a linear probe on layer 12–16 representations achieves >85% accuracy on antecedent resolution, meaning broken chains produce detectable anomalies in the probe's confidence distribution. A cheaper signal is attention sink asymmetry at the eviction boundary: when the first retained token of a coreference chain directs anomalously high attention toward the BOS/sink token rather than toward a legitimate antecedent, it indicates the model has failed to find an in-context resolution and is defaulting to the sink as a null antecedent placeholder — this pattern is measurable in a single forward pass before any decoding step. The practical system design implication, exploited partially in InfLLM and MemGPT-style architectures, is to treat eviction boundary coref violations as retrieval triggers — when a probe detects an unresolved referent, the system re-fetches the evicted span from external memory before generation rather than allowing the model to confabulate resolution.

Empirically, removing attention sink tokens worsens entity tracking when coreference chains are already broken — a counterintuitive result that reveals sinks are not merely parasitic attention attractors but serve an active distributional stabilization function: they provide a low-entropy default target that prevents attention from diffusing chaotically across the retained window when no legitimate antecedent exists. Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM (2023) demonstrated this indirectly by showing that removing the initial sink tokens caused perplexity spikes disproportionate to their information content, but the deeper mechanistic finding is that sink tokens absorb the "excess" attention probability mass that would otherwise be distributed across semantically irrelevant tokens — when sinks are removed, that mass redistributes to the nearest high-frequency tokens, which in a broken-coref context means the dangling referent now falsely binds to whatever token happens to have the highest residual attention weight, typically a semantically prominent but referentially incorrect entity. This reveals that sink function is dual: sinks simultaneously act as (1) a harmless garbage collector for attention in well-formed contexts, and (2) a failure-mode moderator in degraded contexts — their presence caps the severity of spurious resolution by concentrating the erroneous binding at a semantically null target rather than at a plausible wrong entity, meaning hallucinated antecedents become detectable as sink-directed rather than entity-directed attention. The practical diagnostic implication is that sink-directed attention from a definite NP is a cleaner failure signal than diffuse attention: if you strip sinks and re-run the forward pass, broken coref chains that were previously detectable as sink-concentration anomalies now manifest as subtle attention redistribution across legitimate entities, making them harder to detect programmatically. Xiao et al. and follow-up work by Han et al. (2024) on sink ablations in long-context settings converge on a ~12–18% increase in entity tracking error rate when sinks are removed under eviction-boundary coref breaks, suggesting the sink's moderating function is quantitatively significant, not marginal — and this directly indicts eviction policies that treat sink tokens as high-priority retainable tokens, since retaining them for stability while evicting coherence-critical bridging tokens is precisely the trade-off that produces fluent but factually corrupt generation.

The minimal architectural intervention is a learned null-antecedent token — a trainable embedding injected at every eviction boundary whose sole function is to serve as a legitimate resolution target for dangling referents, replacing the accidental sink function with an explicit, semantically typed placeholder that the model can be supervised to use correctly. The deeper architectural fix, requiring slightly more intervention, is soft attention clamping via a learned null-attention head: a dedicated attention head trained to route probability mass to a null state rather than to content tokens when no valid antecedent exists in the window — Miller et al.'s work on "attention dropout regularization" (2023) and the Mistral team's findings on head specialization both suggest that individual heads can be trained toward specific distributional behaviors with minimal interference to other heads, making this feasible without full retraining. What makes both interventions superior to sink reliance is that they make the failure mode semantically legible: a model attending to a trained null token produces a detectable, interpretable signal (this referent is unresolved) rather than the cryptic sink-concentration pattern that requires a separate probe to decode. The reason current architectures evolved sinks rather than null tokens is training distribution: models trained on web-scale text with full context never needed explicit unresolved-referent handling because the antecedent was always present, so the sink emerged as an accidental solution to a problem that only manifests at inference time under compression — Dettmers et al.'s quantization work (2022) inadvertently documented this by showing that sink tokens carry anomalously large activation magnitudes, consistent with their role as trained attractors rather than semantically meaningful content. The information-theoretic upper bound is set by the embedding dimensionality and the mutual information each coreference chain requires: if a boundary token is a d-dimensional float16 vector (d=4096 for LLaMA-class models, giving ~65K bits of raw capacity), and each severed chain requires encoding at minimum the entity type, key attributes, and positional origin of its antecedent — empirically around 50–200 bits per chain based on entropy estimates from OntoNotes entity distributions — a single boundary token could theoretically represent 300–1300 chains, but this is a catastrophically optimistic bound because the model must retrieve specific chain information via attention, not just store it, and retrieval capacity scales far more poorly than storage capacity with superposition. The operative constraint is linear representation interference: Elhage et al.'s superposition hypothesis (2022) and follow-up mechanistic interpretability work establish that when more features than dimensions are packed into a single vector, reconstruction error scales with the square of the number of superposed features for random feature geometries — meaning that beyond roughly d^0.5 ≈ 64 simultaneous chains for a 4096-dim boundary token, retrieval fidelity degrades faster than linearly, and for coreferentially entangled chains (where two chains share entity attributes) interference is catastrophically amplified. Empirically, Chevalier et al.'s AutoCompressor results suggest summary vectors begin losing retrievable content around 4–8 compressed segments with dense entity populations, which translates to roughly 10–30 simultaneous active coreference chains before resolution accuracy drops measurably — a far tighter bound than the raw capacity argument suggests. When this bound is exceeded, eviction policy design must shift from token-level to chain-level granularity: instead of scoring individual tokens for eviction, the policy must track entire coreference chains as atomic eviction units, ensuring that if any token in a chain is evicted, all chain-critical tokens are either co-evicted (and represented jointly in an expanded boundary token set) or co-retained, because partial chain eviction is strictly worse than full eviction when boundary token capacity is saturated — partial eviction wastes boundary token capacity on chains that can't be faithfully resolved anyway. The deeper implication is that exceeding the boundary token capacity bound reveals a phase transition in eviction policy optimality: below the bound, greedy per-token eviction with boundary token compensation is near-optimal; above it, the problem becomes a combinatorial chain packing problem where you must jointly optimize which chains to fully evict, which to fully retain, and how to allocate a fixed budget of boundary tokens across severed chains — a problem structurally identical to the multi-item knapsack problem, which is NP-hard in general but admits good approximations when chain lengths follow the power-law distributions typical of natural language coreference.
